newsitem.title: USA: Digital antitrust threat seen not unusual.
newsitem.headline: Digital antitrust threat seen not unusual.

text.p: Digital Equipment Corp's veiled threat that it may pursue an antitrust lawsuit against Intel Corp is not unusual between warring companies and would be difficult to prove, officials said Monday.

"It's not surprising," said Charles Rule, who headed the antitrust division of the Department of Justice in the late 1980s. "In intellecutal property litigation, it is certainly not unusual to see antitrust counterclaims being threatened or being filed."

In response to an escalating legal battle, Digital general counsel Thomas Siekman said in a letter to Intel's counsel last week that Intel had a monopoly in the microprocessor market and therefore an obligation to provide product information.
Last week, Intel filed suit against Digital, demanding the return of confidential information about its forthcoming products.

"The antitrust laws prohibit Intel, as a monopolist, from denying Digital -- or any other company that designs or manufactures personal computers, workstations or servers based on Intel microprocessors -- access to information of this kind, absent a legitimate business justification," Siekman wrote in the letter to Thomas Dunlap.

"If Intel continues in its pursuit of unlawfully denying Digital access to materials needed by Digital because of Intel's market power, Digital will respond as it believes appropriate," he said in a copy of the letter obtained by Reuters.
Rule, now a lawyer with the Washington law firm Covington & Burling, said that, historically, proving an antitrust infringement has been difficult.
"There are a lot of elements that a plaintiff has to show in order to prevail," he said.
And even if Digital did find sympathy within the Department of Justice, the government has often had difficulty proving antitrust violations, he said.
"I don't think they are going to find sympathy in the absence of good facts to back up a case," he said.
Nathan Brookwood, a microprocessor analyst with Dataquest Inc, said that Intel has been careful not to raise antitrust objections.

"Intel, to the best of my knowledge, has run its business rather meticulously in order to avoid any appearance or provide any trace that their behavior is anti-competitive. Far more than many of its competitors," Brookwood said. "I think (an antitrust case) would be difficult to prove."
